42880960.text: B7 homolog 3 (B7H3) is widely expressed in solid tumors, but its role in the diagnosis of breast cancer is unclear. We aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of [68Ga]Ga-B7H3-BCH PET/CT in breast cancer patients. Methods: Thirty patients with diverse subtypes of breast cancer underwent both [68Ga]Ga-B7H3-BCH and [18F]FDG PET/CT. Immunohistochemical staining for B7H3 was performed in 25 patients. Results: B7H3 positivity was detected in 84% of samples by immunohistochemistry. [68Ga]Ga-B7H3-BCH demonstrated a higher lesion detection rate compared with [18F]FDG (96.8% vs. 92.4%) among 157 lesions. Median SUVmax was 9.5 in strongly positive lesions; bone metastases had the highest uptake (median SUVmax, 10.9). Imaging resulted in changing the stage or treatment in 8 patients. Hormone receptor-positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative lesions showed the highest B7H3 positivity (87.5%) and uptake (median SUVmax, 10.5). Conclusion: [68Ga]Ga-B7H3-BCH PET/CT offers high sensitivity for staging advanced breast cancer and noninvasive B7H3 screening. It may influence clinical decisions and appears to reveal subtype-specific uptake, with a tendency to favor hormone receptor-positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative disease.

42891710.label: Objectives
42891710.text: Pelvic bones exhibit multiple secondary ossification centers during maturation, enabling automated age estimation. This study investigated whether a deep learning model could estimate chronological age from pelvic radiographs across the full pediatric age range.

42891710.label: Materials and methods
42891710.text: This retrospective study included pelvic radiographs from two hospitals for model development, from patients aged between 0 and 18 years. A DenseNet161 model was trained to classify age into 19 1-year interval categories using chronological age as a reference standard and conditional ordinal regression (CORN) loss. External validation was conducted using two independent cohorts, including 541 radiographs from a different department of the same hospital and 203 from an external hospital. External validation was performed on 744 radiographs from two independent cohorts. Model performance was evaluated using the accuracy of predictions within 1 year of the chronological age (ACC@dist = 1) and the mean absolute error (MAE).

42891710.label: Results
42891710.text: A total of 3972 radiographs (median age, 2.5 years; interquartile range, 0-8 years; 2463 males) were included in model development. On the internal test set, the model achieved an MAE of 0.394 years (girls: 0.360; boys: 0.419) and an ACC@dist = 1 of 0.937 (girls: 0.944; boys: 0.931). On the external test sets, the corresponding values were 0.513 years (girls, 0.628; boys, 0.455) and 0.927 (girls, 0.896; boys, 0.943), respectively.

42891710.label: Conclusion
42891710.text: Automated age estimation in children is feasible from pelvic radiography using a deep neural network.

42891710.label: Key points
42891710.text: Question Pelvic radiographs are commonly obtained in children, yet their potential for automated chronological age estimation across the full pediatric age range remains unexplored. Findings A deep learning model estimated chronological age from pelvic radiographs with a mean absolute error of 0.394 and 0.513 years on internal and external test sets, respectively. Clinical relevance Deep learning-based chronological age estimation from pelvic radiographs is feasible across the full pediatric age range. This approach allows clinically relevant skeletal maturation data to be extracted from imaging already acquired for other indications.

42902110.label: Background
42902110.text: The PROMISE framework standardizes PSMA PET interpretation using reference organs, particularly the liver. For hepatobiliary-excreted tracers (e.g., 18F-PSMA-1007), the spleen was proposed as an alternative reference, though without quantitative validation. We evaluated PSMA-ligand uptake patterns among 18F-PSMA-1007, 68Ga-PSMA-11, and 18F-DCFPyL to assess the validity of spleen-based referencing and develop a simple approach that may harmonize 18F-PSMA-1007 liver uptake with that of renally-excreted tracers.

42902110.label: Results
42902110.text: 331 consecutive PSMA PET-CT studies (n = 118/95/118 for 68Ga-PSMA-11/18F-PSMA-1007/18F-DCFPyL) were analyzed: SUVs were retrospectively measured in all studies in reference tissues (blood pool, liver, parotid), with SUVspleen also recorded for 18F-PSMA-1007. SUVliver differed markedly across tracers: 18F-PSMA-1007 (13.95 ± 4.71) > 68Ga-PSMA-11 (7.45 ± 4.59) ≈ 18F-DCFPyL (8.11 ± 1.78), p < 0.01. The elevated 18F-PSMA-1007 liver uptake expanded the PROMISE score-1 range (SUV range between SUVblood pool and SUVliver) and compressed that of score-2 (SUV range between SUVliver and SUVparotid). SUVspleen in this group (12.24 ± 5.67) showed only moderate correlation with SUVliver (r = 0.43) and exceeded SUVliver in 29% of cases, questioning the utility of spleen uptake as a consistent alternative to liver uptake-based cutoff. Linear correction using the inverse ratio of mean SUVliver (18F-PSMA-1007 versus other tracers; factor = 0.56, 95% CI 0.51-0.61) yielded SUVliver-corrected of 7.8 ± 2.63 in the 18F-PSMA-1007 group. Applying SUVspleen as a PSMA score 1-2 cutoff failed to resolve score distribution imbalance, upstaging only 11.8% of score-1 lesions to score-2. By contrast, the use of SUVliver-corrected (SUVliver × 0.56) as this cutoff harmonized the score distribution in the 18F-PSMA-1007 cohort relative to 68Ga-PSMA-11 and 18F-DCFPyL, leading to reclassification of 38.2% of score-1 lesions as score-2.

42902110.label: Conclusion
42902110.text: In PET with 18F-PSMA-1007, PROMISE scoring based on unadjusted liver or spleen uptake systematically underestimates lesion scores. The simple linear correction approach proposed here offers a research avenue for enhancing the consistency of PSMA scoring for improved interpretive standardization.

42944910.label: Purpose
42944910.text: To develop a purely preoperative risk stratification model for anastomotic leakage (AL) after radical gastrectomy using clinical, dual-energy CT (DECT), and body composition variables available before surgery.

42944910.label: Methods
42944910.text: This retrospective study included 439 patients with gastric cancer who underwent radical gastrectomy. Preoperative clinical, DECT, and body composition data were collected. A domain-based predictor selection strategy was used, followed by Firth penalized logistic regression to account for the low event rate. Internal validation was performed using 1000 bootstrap resamples, with an additional full-pipeline bootstrap sensitivity analysis. Model performance was assessed by discrimination, calibration, decision curve analysis (DCA), and risk stratification.

42944910.label: Results
42944910.text: AL occurred in 27 patients (6.15%). The final model included cardia tumor location (OR = 4.44), higher ECV (OR = 1.09 per 1%), and sarcopenia (OR = 3.66). The model showed good discrimination, with an apparent AUC of 0.853 and a bootstrap-corrected AUC of 0.843. Full-pipeline bootstrap sensitivity analysis yielded an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.833. Calibration was acceptable, with a Brier score of 0.050, and DCA suggested potential net benefit. Observed AL rates increased stepwise across low-risk (< 3%), intermediate-risk (3%-10%), and high-risk (≥ 10%) groups: 1.23%, 5.13%, and 22.78%, respectively. The high-risk group comprised 18.0% of the cohort but accounted for 66.7% of all AL events.

42944910.label: Conclusion
42944910.text: A concise model integrating tumor location, DECT-derived ECV, and sarcopenia showed favorable performance for preoperative AL risk stratification after gastrectomy. This internally validated model may help preoperative AL risk stratification, but multicenter external validation and impact analysis are required before implementation.

42957210.text: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT has become the gold standard for staging and restaging prostate cancer, with superior diagnostic accuracy over conventional imaging and established prognostic value. However, there are limited data on whether PSMA PET/CT-improved staging accuracy is associated with improved long-term patient outcomes. This study analyzes the association between PSMA PET/CT at primary staging and overall survival (OS), biochemical recurrence (BCR), and cancer-specific survival (CSS) in a large university hospital cohort at a center where PSMA PET/CT has been clinically available for over 13 y. Methods: This retrospective single-center study included all 11,146 patients with prostate cancer diagnosed between 2013 and 2023. The final analysis cohort consisted of 6999 patients, of whom 505 (7.2%) underwent PSMA PET/CT for primary staging. We classified patients into 3 groups using D'Amico risk classification. Survival analyses were performed using Kaplan-Meier methods and adjusted Cox regression models. To control for selection bias, propensity score matching and overlap weighting were applied. Landmark analysis addressed selection and immortal time biases, and Fine-Gray models accounted for competing risk of death in a BCR analysis. Results: PSMA PET/CT was associated with a longer time to BCR (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.51; 95% CI, 0.38-0.68; P < 0.001), longer CSS (HR = 0.37; 95% CI, 0.22-0.61; P < 0.001), and longer OS (HR = 0.54; 95% CI, 0.40-0.70; P < 0.001). PSMA PET imaging was associated with particularly better outcomes in high-risk patients, especially those treated with radiotherapy. In the radiotherapy group, the HRs were 0.42 for OS, 0.42 for BCR, and 0.25 for CSS (all P < 0.001), whereas no statistically significant association was observed in patients undergoing radical prostatectomy. As the formal interaction test between PSMA PET/CT and treatment modality was not statistically significant, this differential finding should be considered exploratory. Across all 9 sensitivity analyses, HRs were consistently below 1, indicating a uniform direction of benefit. Conclusion: The association observed in this large real-world cohort supports the clinical value of PSMA PET/CT for primary staging. Findings were particularly favorable among high-risk patients undergoing radiotherapy, although this subgroup difference should be interpreted as exploratory given the nonsignificant interaction test. These results support a potential role for PSMA PET/CT in improving patient selection and detecting oligometastatic disease, enabling higher precision in treatment planning.

43020610.text: Whole-body prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT segmentation remains challenging: manual contouring is unsustainable, and image-only artificial intelligence models often misclassify physiologic uptake as malignant, causing high false-positive rates. These limitations underscore the need for segmentation strategies that incorporate the nuclear medicine expertise encoded in PET/CT reports but not used by current models. We investigated whether routine PET/CT reports improve automated lesion segmentation for prostate cancer. Methods: We developed a language-guided 3-dimensional SegResNet fusing report text with 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT image features, encoding report semantics via 4 strategies (BiomedVLP, RadGraph, GPT-raw, GPT-engineered) compared with an image-only model (baseline). Of 320 patients who underwent 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT, 297 studies were available; 13 were excluded for missing reports or incomplete image-mask pairs, leaving 284 for analysis, split at the patient level into 243 development cases and a fixed 41-case held-out test set. Metrics included Dice, intersection over union (IoU), precision, recall, average symmetric surface distance, 95th percentile Hausdorff distance, surface Dice similarity at 5 mm, and lesion-level false positives, using 3 matching criteria (any overlap; 1-to-1 maximum IoU matching, IoU ≥ 0.5; and correct localization of the SUVmax voxel). Significance was assessed using paired 1-sided Wilcoxon tests with Holm adjustment. Results: Report guidance consistently reduced false positives and improved whole-mask boundary agreement. False-positive lesions were reduced by nearly 4 per patient with BiomedVLP and by approximately 3 per patient with RadGraph and GPT-raw. Average symmetric surface distance decreased from 105.4 ± 62.5 mm (image only) to 23.4 ± 18.2 mm with BiomedVLP, 36.9 ± 22.4 mm with RadGraph, and 36.3 ± 26.4 mm with GPT-raw; 95th percentile Hausdorff distance improved from 455.0 ± 169.3 mm to 123.8 ± 80.3 mm with BiomedVLP, and surface Dice similarity at 5 mm increased from 0.638 ± 0.172 to 0.705 ± 0.181. However, when these surface metrics were recomputed on matched true-positive lesions only using the same 3 criteria, no language-guided model differed significantly from the image-only model for any surface metric (all Holm-adjusted P = 1.0), indicating that the whole-mask improvements were attributable to false-positive suppression rather than genuine gains in contour accuracy on correctly detected lesions. Precision increased for BiomedVLP (0.099) and RadGraph (0.060), with a modest decrease in voxel-level recall (-0.051, BiomedVLP), reflecting a precision-recall trade-off from suppression of spurious uptake. Dice improved by 0.032 but was borderline significant; IoU increased for BiomedVLP (0.036). Lesion-level sensitivity changed by no more than 0.04 for all models and did not reach significance. Total lesion PSMA remained highly correlated with manual measurements (r ≥ 0.85), whereas PSMA tumor volume correlations were more variable across models (r = 0.37-0.70). Conclusion: The integration of PET/CT report semantics into automated PSMA PET/CT segmentation substantially reduced false-positive lesions and preserved total lesion PSMA agreement with manual measurements; a matched true-positive-only reanalysis indicated that the accompanying whole-mask boundary-agreement gains reflected false-positive suppression rather than improved contour accuracy on correctly detected lesions. This approach may reduce manual cleanup and support more reliable quantitative workflows, although precision gains should be weighed against a modest recall reduction. External validation, extension of the true-positive-only analysis to independent cohorts, and PSMA-specific language pretraining are warranted.

43079060.text: Small and disseminated lesions within the bone marrow remain challenging to detect and eradicate in multiple myeloma (MM), highlighting the need for targeted approaches capable of both sensitive imaging and localized radiation delivery. CD38 is highly expressed on malignant plasma cells and represents an established target in MM, but CD38-directed radiopharmaceuticals with rapid tumor targeting and favorable pharmacokinetics remain limited. Here, we developed CP021, a high-affinity CD38-targeting cyclic peptide, and evaluated [⁶⁸Ga]Ga-DOTA-CP021 for PET imaging, together with [¹⁷⁷Lu]Lu-DOTA-CP021 and [²¹²Pb]Pb-DOTAM-CP021 for targeted radionuclide therapy in preclinical MM models.MethodsDOTA-CP021 was labeled with ⁶⁸Ga or ¹⁷⁷Lu and DOTAM-CP021 with ²¹²Pb. Radiochemical properties, PET imaging, biodistribution, pharmacokinetics, dosimetry, therapeutic efficacy, and safety were evaluated in MM xenograft models.ResultsAll radioconjugates showed > 95% radiochemical purity and good stability. [⁶⁸Ga]Ga-DOTA-CP021 demonstrated CD38-dependent tumor uptake; at 60 min, uptake in CD38-high MOLP-8 xenografts was 12.35 ± 1.37%ID/g, 1.8- and 3.1-fold higher than in MM.1 S and U266B1 tumors, respectively. [¹⁷⁷Lu]Lu-DOTA-CP021 produced activity-dependent tumor growth inhibition and prolonged survival. Repeated [²¹²Pb]Pb-DOTAM-CP021 further improved tumor control, extending median survival to 36.5 and 47 days at cumulative activities of 0.555 and 1.11 MBq, respectively, versus 16 days with PBS (P < 0.001). No overt treatment-related toxicity was observed.ConclusionCP021 provides a versatile CD38-targeted radiotheranostic platform combining rapid molecular imaging with β- and α-particle therapy. Its performance across radionuclides supports further development for detecting and treating CD38-positive MM lesions.
